CHAPTER XXXIV

THE END


In the early summer of next year two old men sat reading their
newspapers after breakfast upon the terrace of Broad Place. The elder of
the two turned over a sheet.

"I see Osman Digna's back at Suakin," said he. "There's likely to be
some fighting."

"Oh," said the other, "he will not do much harm." And he laid down his
paper. The quiet English country-side vanished from before his eyes. He
saw only the white city by the Red Sea shimmering in the heat, the brown
plains about it with their tangle of halfa grass, and in the distance
the hills towards Khor Gwob.

"A stuffy place Suakin, eh, Sutch?" said General Feversham.

"Appallingly stuffy. I heard of an officer who went down on parade at
six o'clock of the morning there, sunstruck in the temples right through
a regulation helmet. Yes, a town of dank heat! But I was glad to be
there--very glad," he said with some feeling.

"Yes," said Feversham, briskly; "ibex, eh?"

"No," replied Sutch. "All the ibex had been shot off by the English
garrison for miles round."

"No? Something to do, then. That's it?"

"Yes, that's it, Feversham. Something to do."

And both men busied themselves again over their papers. But in a little
while a footman brought to each a small pile of letters. General
Feversham ran over his envelopes with a quick eye, selected one letter,
and gave a grunt of satisfaction. He took a pair of spectacles from a
case and placed them upon his nose.

"From Ramelton?" asked Sutch, dropping his newspaper on to the terrace.

"From Ramelton," answered Feversham. "I'll light a cigar first."

He laid the letter down on the garden table which stood between his
companion and himself, drew a cigar-case from his pocket, and in spite
of the impatience of Lieutenant Sutch, proceeded to cut and light it
with the utmost deliberation. The old man had become an epicure in this
respect. A letter from Ramelton was a luxury to be enjoyed with all the
accessories of comfort which could be obtained. He made himself
comfortable in his chair, stretched out his legs, and smoked enough of
his cigar to assure himself that it was drawing well. Then he took up
his letter again and opened it.

"From him?" asked Sutch.

"No; from her."

"Ah!"

General Feversham read the letter through slowly, while Lieutenant Sutch
tried not to peep at it across the table. When the general had finished
he turned back to the first page, and began it again.

"Any news?" said Sutch, with a casual air.

"They are very pleased with the house now that it's rebuilt."

"Anything more?"

"Yes. Harry's finished the sixth chapter of his history of the war."

"Good!" said Sutch. "You'll see, he'll do that well. He has imagination,
he knows the ground, he was present while the war went on. Moreover, he
was in the bazaars, he saw the under side of it."

"Yes. But you and I won't read it, Sutch," said Feversham. "No; I am
wrong. You may, for you can give me a good many years."

He turned back to his letter and again Sutch asked:--

"Anything more?"

"Yes. They are coming here in a fortnight."

"Good," said Sutch. "I shall stay."

He took a turn along the terrace and came back. He saw Feversham sitting
with the letter upon his knees and a frown of great perplexity upon his
face.

"You know, Sutch, I never understood," he said. "Did you?"

"Yes, I think I did."

Sutch did not try to explain. It was as well, he thought, that Feversham
never would understand. For he could not understand without much
self-reproach.

"Do you ever see Durrance?" asked the general, suddenly.

"Yes, I see a good deal of Durrance. He is abroad just now."

Feversham turned towards his friend.

"He came to Broad Place when you went to Suakin, and talked to me for
half an hour. He was Harry's best man. Well, that too I never
understood. Did you?"

"Yes, I understood that as well."

"Oh!" said General Feversham. He asked for no explanations, but, as he
had always done, he took the questions which he did not understand and
put them aside out of his thoughts. But he did not turn to his other
letters. He sat smoking his cigar, and looked out across the summer
country and listened to the sounds rising distinctly from the fields.
Sutch had read through all of his correspondence before Feversham spoke
again.

"I have been thinking," he said. "Have you noticed the date of the
month, Sutch?" and Sutch looked up quickly.

"Yes," said he, "this day next week will be the anniversary of our
attack upon the Redan, and Harry's birthday."

"Exactly," replied Feversham. "Why shouldn't we start the Crimean nights
again?"

Sutch jumped up from his chair.

"Splendid!" he cried. "Can we muster a tableful, do you think?"

"Let's see," said Feversham, and ringing a handbell upon the table, sent
the servant for the Army List. Bending over that Army List the two
veterans may be left.

But of one other figure in this story a final word must be said. That
night, when the invitations had been sent out from Broad Place, and no
longer a light gleamed from any window of the house, a man leaned over
the rail of a steamer anchored at Port Said and listened to the song of
the Arab coolies as they tramped up and down the planks with their coal
baskets between the barges and the ship's side. The clamour of the
streets of the town came across the water to his ears. He pictured to
himself the flare of braziers upon the quays, the lighted port-holes,
and dark funnels ahead and behind in the procession of the anchored
ships. Attended by a servant, he had come back to the East again. Early
the next morning the steamer moved through the canal, and towards the
time of sunset passed out into the chills of the Gulf of Suez. Kassassin,
Tel-el-Kebir, Tamai, Tamanieb, the attack upon McNeil's
zareeba--Durrance lived again through the good years of his activity,
the years of plenty. Within that country on the west the long
preparations were going steadily forward which would one day roll up the
Dervish Empire and crush it into dust. Upon the glacis of the ruined
fort of Sinkat, Durrance had promised himself to take a hand in that
great work, but the desert which he loved had smitten and cast him out.
But at all events the boat steamed southwards into the Red Sea. Three
nights more, and though he would not see it, the Southern Cross would
lift slantwise into the sky.




       *       *       *       *       *


By A. E. W. Mason

THE COURTSHIP OF MAURICE BUCKLER

_A ROMANCE_


Being a record of the growth of an English Gentleman, during the years
of 1685-1687, under strange and difficult circumstances, written some
while afterward in his own hand, and now edited by A. E. W. MASON


Philadelphia Evening Bulletin: In spirit and color it reminds us of the
very remarkable books of Mr. Conon Doyle. The author has measurably
caught the fascinating diction of the seventeenth century, and the
strange adventures with which the story is filled are of a sufficiently
perilous order to entertain the most Homeric mind.

Boston Courier: In this elaborately ingenious narrative the adventures
recorded are various and exciting enough to suit the most exacting
reader. The incidents recited are of extreme interest, and are not drawn
out into noticeable tenuity.

The Outlook: "The Courtship of Maurice Buckler" is not only full of
action and stimulating to curiosity, but tells a quite original plot in
a clever way. Perhaps in its literary kinship it approaches more closely
to "The Prisoner of Zenda" than to any other recent novel, but there is
no evidence of imitation; the resemblance is in the spirit and dash of
the narrative. The merit of this story is not solely in its grasp on the
reader's attention and its exciting situations; it is written in
excellent English, the dialogue is natural and brisk, the individual
characters stand out clearly, and the flavor of the time is well
preserved.

"And what harm can he do?" asked the younger man, Lieutenant Sutch, setting his paper down with a soft thud. His gaze had already drifted away from the tranquil English lawn. To his mind, the rolling hills of Kent had dissolved. Now, standing before him was the blinding white glare of Suakin, shimmering under a relentless sun. He saw the endless, dusty plains tangled with halfa grass, stretching out until the jagged silhouette of the hills near Khor Gwob pierced the horizon.

"A stifling place, surely?" General Feversham remarked, his voice brisk.

"Appalling," Sutch agreed. "I heard tell of an officer who collapsed on parade at six in the morning, struck down by the sun right through the steel of his helmet. It is a hell of a damp heat." Yet, despite his words, a profound sense of gratitude warmed his chest. "However, I am glad I was there," he admitted, his tone shifting with genuine emotion. "Very glad."

"Indeed," Feversham nodded, leaning forward slightly. "And did you find your ibex?"

"No," Sutch replied firmly. "Every single ibex within a mile's radius had been shot down by the English garrison."

"So? What else kept you busy?"

"There was something to do," Sutch said, his voice steady. "Just that."

General Feversham swept his fingers over the envelopes, his eyes moving with practiced speed, before selecting one and letting out a low grunt of contentment. From his case, he produced a pair of spectacles, adjusting them carefully onto his nose.

"A letter from Ramelton?" Sutch asked, lowering his own paper.

"From Ramelton," Feversham confirmed. "First, however, a cigar."

He laid the letter down on the wooden table between them, reached into his pocket, and with deliberate slowness—despite Sutch's visible impatience—he cut and lit the tobacco. An old man like Feversham treated a letter from home not merely as information, but as a feast to be savored with every accessory of comfort. He settled deeper into his chair, extended his legs, and smoked long enough to ensure the draw was perfect before finally unrolling the paper.

"To him?" Sutch ventured.

"No," Feversham murmured. "To her."

Sutch let out a sharp intake of breath. "Ah."

Feversham read the letter through once, his expression unreadable, then paused, turning back to the beginning to read it again.

"Is there anything new?" Sutch asked, feigning a casual indifference.

"They are delighted with the house now that it stands rebuilt."

"And nothing else?"

"Yes. Harry has completed the sixth chapter of his history of the war."

"Excellent!" Sutch exclaimed. "You'll see how well he does it. He possesses true imagination. He knows the terrain intimately, having walked it while the fighting raged. Furthermore, he wandered the bazaars; he has seen the underside of things."

"Yes," Feversham conceded. "But I doubt you and I will read it, Sutch."

"No," Feversham corrected himself immediately, a smile touching his lips. "That is wrong. You may read it, for you still have many years ahead of me."

He folded the letter and set it aside. Again, Sutch pressed gently. "Anything further?"

"Yes. They are arriving here in two weeks' time."

"That is splendid," Sutch said, his face lighting up. "I shall remain."

He paced along the terrace, returning to his seat where he found Feversham staring at the letter with a look of deep perplexity etched upon his brow.

"You know, Sutch," the General said, breaking the silence, "there are certain things I never fully grasped. Did you?"

"Yes, I believe so," Sutch offered quietly.

He did not attempt to elaborate. It seemed wise, he felt, that Feversham should never understand the weight of those moments, for understanding required a burden of self-reproach that the General simply could not bear.

"Do you ever see Captain Durrance?" Feversham asked suddenly.

"Yes, I see him often. He is currently abroad."

Feversham turned to face his friend. "He visited Broad Place when you departed for Suakin. We spoke for half an hour. He was Harry's best man. Well, that, too, remains a mystery to me. Did you comprehend it?"

"Yes, I understood that perfectly," Sutch lied smoothly.

"Oh!" Feversham sighed, the question passing through him like smoke. As always, he chose to set such unanswerable mysteries aside, burying them beneath the surface of his thoughts. Sutch had gone through every envelope in the stack before the General spoke again.

"I have been reflecting," Feversham said, his eyes brightening. "Have you noticed the date, Sutch?"

Sutch looked up sharply. "Yes," he replied. "Next day marks the anniversary of our assault on the Redan—and Harry's birthday."

"Precisely," Feversham smiled. "Why not revive the 'Crimean Nights' again?"

Sutch sprang from his chair. "Splendid idea!" he cried. "Do you suppose we can gather a table full of guests?"

"Let us see," Feversham said, ringing the handbell on the table. The servant appeared instantly, summoned to fetch the Army List. The two veterans bent over the book, planning their reunion.

The roar of the town drifted across the water to him—a chaotic symphony of street cries and market noise. In his mind, he visualized the flare of braziers lining the quays, the glowing portholes, and the black funnels of the anchored ships forming a silent procession.

Attended by a servant, he had returned to the East. By early morning, the steamer pushed through the canal, and as sunset approached, it emerged into the chilling waters of the Gulf of Suez. Within the vast lands to the west, preparations were underway, steady and inexorable, destined one day to roll up the Dervish Empire and grind it to dust. On the scarred ramparts of the ruined fort of Sinkat, Durrance had vowed to join that grand endeavor, but the desert he loved had rejected him, casting him out. Sutch looked up sharply. "Yes," he replied. "Next day marks the anniversary of our assault on the Redan—and Harry's birthday."

"Precisely," Feversham smiled. "Why not revive the 'Crimean Nights' again?"

Sutch sprang from his chair. "Splendid idea!" he cried. "Do you suppose we can gather a table full of guests?"

"Let us see," Feversham said, ringing the handbell on the table. The servant appeared instantly, summoned to fetch the Army List. The two veterans bent over the book, planning their reunion.

Yet, the story of this chapter would not end with them. That same night, after the invitations had been dispatched from Broad Place and the last light extinguished from the windows, a solitary figure leaned against the railing of a steamer anchored at Port Said. The man listened to the rhythmic chant of the Arab coolies, whose footsteps echoed as they carried coal baskets between the barges and the ship's side. The roar of the town drifted across the water to him—a chaotic symphony of street cries and market noise. In his mind, he visualized the flare of braziers lining the quays, the glowing portholes, and the black funnels of the anchored ships forming a silent procession.

Attended by a servant, he had returned to the East. By early morning, the steamer pushed through the canal, and as sunset approached, it emerged into the chilling waters of the Gulf of Suez. Kassassin, Tel-el-Kebir, Tamai, Tamanieb—the memory of McNeil's zareeba flashed before his eyes. Captain Durrance relived those golden years of his activity, the era of plenty. Within the vast lands to the west, preparations were underway, steady and inexorable, destined one day to roll up the Dervish Empire and grind it to dust. On the scarred ramparts of the ruined fort of Sinkat, Durrance had vowed to join that grand endeavor, but the desert he loved had rejected him, casting him out. Nevertheless, the boat steamed southward into the Red Sea. Just three nights hence, though he would not witness it, the Southern Cross would rise obliquely into the twilight sky.
